There are two types of tectonic plates that make up Earth's crust. There are continental plates, which are composed of silicates and lighter minerals, and there are also oceanic plates which are primarily composed of basalts and gabbros, which are rich in iron, and magnesium. The oceanic plates are more dense despite the fact that they are generally much thinner than continental plates, so they don't float as high on the mantle as continental plates do.

Oceanic plates usually form at spreading ridges in the ocean, and move outward. The best example of this today is the mid-atlantic spreading ridge (https://images.duckduckgo.com/iu/?u=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.windows2universe.org%2Fteacher_resources%2Fmagnetism%2Fmid_atlantic_ridge_10_inch.jpg&f=1)) When two plates start moving away from each other it creates a void on top of the mantle rock. If you recall from my previous post, mantle rock is like very dense jello. The reason that it acts like jello underground, and like fluid above ground has a lot to do with the downward pressure from the rocks above it. When this pressure is removed the mantle becomes less viscous, and more liquid. This is often referred to as magma. The magma rises to the surface where it becomes lava and it cools, turning into ocean floor.

Continental plates are less dense than oceanic plates. This is the primary reason that most of the continental plates are above sea level. Lots of people have ideas on how continental plates formed, but no one can prove their idea is right. I don't know enough yet to feel comfortable speculating on how they formed, but I can tell you that continental plates are far less likely to be destroyed.

Yesterday's post was about mantle convection, and how it acts like a conveyor belt that the oceanic and continental plates ride on. Obviously these plates are very tightly packed together, so if they are going to move, they are going to hit each other. When two oceanic plates hit each other, the older plate will subduct below the younger one. This is because the older plate has had more time to cool down, and so is less dense than the younger one. In fact, very old oceanic crust will become so dense that it starts trying to sink into the mantle even if it isn't around another plate to subduct.

When oceanic plates meet continental plates the oceanic plate will always subduct below the continental plate. The angle of subduction is determined by the latent heat in the oceanic plate though. The western coast of the US recently (on the geologic time scale) overrode some very young oceanic plate (Juan de Fuca, it's still in the process of overriding it in the Pacific Northwest). That oceanic plate scraped along the bottom of the North American plate because it was so light, it didn't want to sink. This is why there is a chain of volcanoes in inland Arizona (Sunset Crater is the most famous). Here is a diagram of the Juan de Fuca being subducted in the Pacific Northwest: https://images.duckduckgo.com/iu/?u=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.earthmagazine.org%2Fsites%2Fearthmagazine.org%2Ffiles%2F2014-Jun%2FCascadiaSubductionv2.png&f=1

Finally, we get to continental to continental plate collisions. There is one going on right now in southern Asia. India is plowing into China, and the result is the Himalayan mountain chain. What is really cool about this collision is that if you look at it on a long time scale, it is remarkably similar to an ocean wave crashing on a beach. The mountains have gotten so large that gravity is causing them to collapse, mostly on the Chinese side of the collision. An ancient example of two continental plates colliding is at the Caucus Mountains in western Russia. This is the range that is left over from the collision between Europe and Asia. Hawaii is roughly in the position of where the next continent to continent collision will be, where the west coast of North America is scheduled to collide with China in roughly 250 million years. As far as anyone knows, continental plates do not subduct. They formed early in earth's history and have not been recycled the way that oceanic plates have.
